explanations.explanation: Miriam it is. The text says it plainly: "There Miriam died and was buried." Moses and Aaron's sister is laid to rest at Kadesh, and the text gives it just one short sentence. I think that's a heavy way to start the day.

Jochebed is a real name from this family, friend. She's Moses' mother, the one who bore Aaron, Moses and their sister Miriam (Numbers 26:59). But Numbers 20:1 doesn't say she died at Kadesh. The one it names is Miriam, and I think that one hurts.

Zipporah is Moses' wife (Exodus 18:2), so I see why the name came to mind. But this verse never mentions her. It says, "There Miriam died and was buried." Miriam is the one buried at Kadesh, and I think this is a sad verse.

Water, friend. "Now there was no water for the congregation." Everything else in this scene grows out of that one problem. People can put up with a lot, but a whole crowd with empty cups gets loud fast.

Firewood would be a rough shortage, I'll give you that. But the text says there was no water for the congregation. Verse 2 starts the trouble right there. A campfire with nothing to drink next to it is just a very warm complaint.

Shelter's a fair guess, but the text doesn't say anything about that. It says there was no water for the congregation. That's the whole problem in verse 2. You can have the nicest roof around and still be thirsty under it.
Not this time, friend. The text says they gathered against Moses and Aaron, not alongside them. Then the people quarreled with Moses. Nobody in verses 2 and 3 is praying yet. They're complaining.
False is right. The text says "they gathered against Moses and Aaron." Against, not alongside. Verse 3 adds that the people quarreled with Moses. It's a crowd with a complaint, not a prayer meeting.

Livestock is it. The people ask why they were brought into the wilderness "for us and our livestock to die here." Their animals are on their minds too. I think when the animals are thirsty, the worry gets louder.

I get why you'd go there, but the text doesn't mention children in this complaint. The people say they were brought here "for us and our livestock to die here." The animals are the ones named alongside them. I only know what the verse says, and it says livestock.

Elders aren't in this complaint, friend. The people say they were brought into the wilderness "for us and our livestock to die here." The ones named next to them are their livestock. That's the answer the verse gives.

Egypt. The people ask, "Why have you led us up out of Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?" They're pointing back at where they came from and then at where they are now. A thirsty crowd will compare anything to anything.

Midian's a real place, but it's not the one in this complaint. The people say, "Why have you led us up out of Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?" Egypt is the place they name. They're looking backward, and they're not happy about the view ahead.
Moab isn't the place they name, friend. The complaint in verse 5 says, "Why have you led us up out of Egypt…" Egypt is where they say they were led up from. Moab doesn't come up in this scene at all.

The glory of the LORD, that's it. Moses and Aaron fall facedown, and "the glory of the LORD appeared to them." They walked away from the quarreling crowd and got an answer at the Tent of Meeting. That is a good place to take a problem.
A pillar of fire is a big image, so I get it. But verse 6 doesn't say that here. It says Moses and Aaron fell facedown, "and the glory of the LORD appeared to them." That's the answer.

That's a dramatic picture, friend, but it's not in this verse. The text says they fell facedown, "and the glory of the LORD appeared to them." Nobody is described holding a sword here. The glory of the LORD is what appears.

Speak to it. The LORD says, "You and your brother Aaron are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water." Keep that instruction in your pocket, because it matters in a few verses. It's a short command, so it's easy to remember.

No oil in this instruction, friend. The LORD says, "You and your brother Aaron are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water." Speaking is the command. Remember it, because it comes back.
No shovels needed here. The LORD says Moses and Aaron "are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water." The instruction is to speak. Hold onto that.
You rebels. Moses says, "Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?" Those are sharp words to say to a whole assembly. Notice the question that follows them, too.
That would've been a gentler speech, friend, but it's not what the text says. Moses says, "Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?" Rebels is the word he uses for them.
Close in tone, maybe, but not the word. Moses says, "Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?" Rebels is the name he calls them. It's a blunt way to open.
Strikes. "Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff." Remember what the LORD told them to do to the rock a few verses earlier. The text says what Moses did, and it says twice.

Touching would've been a softer move, friend. But the text says Moses "raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff." That's a raised hand, not a gentle tap. Put that next to what the LORD actually said to do.
Pointing is a quiet move, and the text isn't quiet here. Moses "raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff." Struck is the word. Twice is the count.
True. "A great amount of water gushed out, and the congregation and their livestock were able to drink." The thirsty crowd and their animals all got water. The scene doesn't end here, though.

Not false, friend. The text says "a great amount of water gushed out, and the congregation and their livestock were able to drink." The water came, and the people and the animals drank. What happens next is the part that stings.
That's it. The LORD says, "Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites…" That is the reason the LORD gives. It's a serious verse, so take it slowly.

That's not what the LORD names, friend. He says, "Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites…" The thing they didn't trust Him to do is show His holiness. Leading through the wilderness isn't the reason given.

Battles aren't part of this verse. The LORD says, "Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites…" That's what they didn't trust Him to do. No enemies in sight at the rock, just a thirsty crowd and a stick.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." That's said to both Moses and Aaron. So they won't be the ones leading the assembly in. It's a heavy word for these two.

False is right. The LORD says to Moses and Aaron, "…you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them." The land is still given to the people, but these two won't be the ones bringing them in. Verse 13 then names the place, Meribah.
